title: Programming Languages and Frameworks
answer: The languages AI is written in and the frameworks built on top of them, tracked by adoption, releases, licence, and integrations.

reading.body:
The category holds 36 tracked entries across three groups, and the largest is AI frameworks at 17, not languages or inference engines.

The split is 7 programming languages, 17 AI frameworks, and 12 inference engines. Frameworks outnumber languages by more than two to one. That is the shape of a field where the hard part has moved from writing code to wiring components together, and where the serving layer is substantial enough to be tracked as its own group rather than folded into frameworks.

For AI specifically, the inference engine count is the one that connects to compute. Serving software is what turns a purchased accelerator into usable throughput, so a dozen tracked engines is a measure of how much effort goes into extracting work from hardware already bought. The language list is short and stable by comparison, which fits a field that settled on Python early and has not replaced it.

What this does not cover is adoption, releases, licence, or integrations, despite those being the stated tracking dimensions. The data gives names and counts only. It also carries no dates for any entry, so nothing here shows whether any of these groups is growing or shrinking.
